response.executive_summary:
This assessment reviewed the Parcelworks platform architecture as described in the platform-overview.md document, including its customer- and driver-facing interfaces, core application services, data stores, and integrations with external providers.

The assessment produced one approved finding. This is a high-severity issue concerning the risk that a compromised staff SSO account with Admin Console access could be used to view and modify all orders and customer records, directly affecting the confidentiality and integrity of those records. No documentation gaps were formally recorded.

The documentation also described several platform-level controls: interactive user authentication is delegated to an SSO provider via the Identity Service, core services authenticate to the Message Bus with per-service credentials, and the Orders Database and Tracking Store in the data zone are reachable only from the core zone. However, many high- and medium-priority open questions remain, particularly around retention and deletion policies for Data Warehouse contents, Object Storage, and logs; encryption in transit and at rest for internal data flows and stores; authorization granularity and audit logging for the Admin Console; CI/CD and secrets handling for services and external integrations; tenant isolation across data stores and Object Storage; external provider behaviour and inbound event handling; and whether any AI or model-based processing is present. Until these questions are resolved, the strength and coverage of several important controls cannot be fully determined.
response.system_overview:
Parcelworks is a multi-component platform serving several actor types: customers, drivers, staff operators, carrier partners, and external service providers. Customers access the system through the Customer Portal, drivers interact via the Driver Mobile Application, and staff operators use the Admin Console. Client traffic from the Customer Portal and driver application enters through the API Gateway at the edge of the platform, across the trust boundary between the public internet and the edge zone.

Interactive authentication for customers, drivers, and staff is handled by an Identity Service that delegates sign-in to an SSO provider over OpenID Connect, then issues short-lived internal tokens which core services verify. This SSO provider is treated as an external actor. The API Gateway also communicates with the Mobile Gateway and the Identity Service as part of handling these authenticated requests.

Within the core zone, multiple application services coordinate platform functionality. The Order Service writes operational data to the Orders Database and publishes events to the Message Bus. The Mobile Gateway publishes scan events from the driver application to the Message Bus, which delivers them to the Tracking Service; the Tracking Service persists parcel tracking data into the Tracking Store. The Dispatch Service sends assignments to the Mobile Gateway for delivery to drivers. The Label Service generates shipping labels and stores label PDFs in Object Storage, and the Notification Service sends notification messages via a Messaging Provider Service. The Billing Service communicates with a Payment Provider Service, and the Carrier Link component integrates with Carrier Partner APIs. These external providers (messaging, payment, SSO, and carrier partners) are reached across the trust boundary between the core and operations environment and external providers.

Data is stored in several back-end systems. Orders and customer records reside in the Orders Database, with nightly copies taken into a Data Warehouse for post-processing. Parcel tracking data is stored in the Tracking Store. Object Storage holds shipping label PDFs and proof-of-delivery photos. A Shared Application Log captures rendered notification message bodies, and the platform maintains message bus service credentials as a sensitive asset. The Message Bus provides asynchronous communication between services, using per-service credentials for publish/subscribe access. The Orders Database and Tracking Store are located in a data zone that is reachable only from the core zone, reflecting a network segmentation control between core and data zones.
response.risk_summary:
The approved findings concentrate risk on privileged access to the Admin Console. The single high-severity finding concludes that if a staff SSO account with Admin Console access is compromised, an attacker could use the console’s full-access capabilities to read and exfiltrate all orders and customer records and arbitrarily modify orders and addresses. This directly threatens both the confidentiality and integrity of orders and customer records, a primary asset for the platform.

This finding rests on specific assumptions about how administrator access is granted and protected, including reliance on an is_admin flag to restrict Admin Console functionality to staff operator accounts and the use of the same SSO sign-in path for both customers and staff. Multiple open questions focus on related areas such as multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts, additional authorization or role separation within the Admin Console, and the presence and quality of audit logging for administrative actions. Because these aspects are not yet fully documented, the effectiveness of existing controls against compromise or misuse of admin-capable accounts cannot be conclusively assessed.

Beyond the Admin Console, the confirmed controls show that authentication is centralized through an SSO provider, core services authenticate individually to the Message Bus, and core-to-data zone access is restricted. However, a large set of open questions leaves several important risk areas indeterminate. These include data protection and lifecycle management for the Orders Database, Tracking Store, Data Warehouse, Object Storage, and Shared Application Log (encryption in transit and at rest, retention and deletion, and tenant separation); the security of CI/CD and secrets handling for components such as the Deploy Runner and Message Bus credentials; the scope and limitations of external integrations with messaging, payment, and carrier providers, including any inbound webhooks or events; and whether any AI or model-based components are present and how they are controlled. As a result, while only one high-severity weakness met the bar for an approved finding, the unresolved questions mean that the overall risk posture, particularly around data protection, privileged access, and third-party integrations, remains partly undetermined.

limitations.text: The analysis and conclusions for finding fnd-001 depend on stated assumptions about how administrative access is implemented. Specifically, the assessment assumes that an is_admin flag on user records reliably restricts Admin Console functionality to a defined set of staff operator accounts, and that staff use the same SSO sign-in path as customers so that the access path for administrators is not stronger than customer access. If these assumptions are inaccurate or change, the applicability, severity, and appropriate response to fnd-001 may differ from what is described in this report.
